paragraphs: I shall perhaps be reminded here of a common saying, "that where annual elections end, tyranny begins." It has often been remarked that sayings that become proverbs are generally founded in reason. It is no less true that, once they are established, they are often applied to cases the reason behind them does not reach. The case before us is proof enough. What is the reason this proverb is founded on? No one will expose himself to ridicule by pretending that there is any natural connection between the sun or the seasons and the length of time human virtue can stand up to the temptations of power. Happily for mankind, liberty is not tied to any single point of time in this respect. It lies between extremes that leave room for all the variations that the different situations and circumstances of civil society may require. The election of public officials might be daily, weekly or monthly, as well as annual, if that were found expedient; in some instances it actually has been. And if circumstances may call for a departure from the rule in one direction, why not in the other? Look at the periods established among ourselves for electing the most numerous branches of the State legislatures. They differ here no more than they do in the elections of other civil officials. In Connecticut and Rhode Island the periods are half-yearly. In the other States, except South Carolina, they are annual. In South Carolina they are biennial, as is proposed for the federal government. That is a difference of four to one between the longest and shortest periods. Yet it would not be easy to show that Connecticut or Rhode Island is better governed, or enjoys more rational liberty, than South Carolina. Nor would it be easy to show that any of these States is distinguished in those respects, or by those causes, from the States whose elections differ from both.

I can find only one ground for this doctrine, and it is wholly inapplicable to our case. Americans understand well the important distinction between a Constitution established by the people and unalterable by the government, and a law established by the government and alterable by the government. In any other country this distinction seems to have been little understood and less observed. Wherever the supreme power of legislation has resided, people have supposed that it also held a full power to change the form of the government. Even in Great Britain, where the principles of political and civil liberty have been most discussed and where we hear most about the rights of the Constitution, it is maintained that the authority of Parliament is transcendent and uncontrollable, as much over the Constitution as over the ordinary objects of legislation. Parliament has accordingly, in several instances, changed some of the most fundamental articles of the government by legislative acts. In particular, it has several times changed the period of election. On the last occasion it not only brought in septennial elections in place of triennial ones, but in the same act extended its own term four years beyond what the people had elected it for. Attention to these dangerous practices has naturally alarmed the devotees of free government, of which frequent elections are the cornerstone, and has led them to look for some security for liberty against the danger it faces. Where no Constitution paramount to the government existed or could be had, no constitutional security like the one established in the United States could be tried. Some other security had to be found. What better security would the case allow than to pick some simple and familiar portion of time and appeal to it as a standard, by which to measure the danger of innovations, to fix the national sentiment and to unite patriotic efforts? The simplest and most familiar portion of time suited to the purpose was a year. Hence a laudable zeal, seeking to put up some barrier against the gradual innovations of an unlimited government, has taught the doctrine that the approach of tyranny can be measured by how far one departs from the fixed point of annual elections. But what need is there to apply this expedient to a government limited, as the federal government will be, by the authority of a paramount Constitution? Or who will claim that the liberties of the people of America will be less secure under biennial elections, unalterably fixed by such a Constitution, than those of any other nation would be where elections were annual, or even more frequent, but could be altered by the ordinary power of the government?
The second question stated is whether biennial elections are necessary or useful. Several very obvious considerations show that the answer should be yes.

No one can be a competent legislator unless, besides upright intentions and sound judgment, he has a certain amount of knowledge of the subjects he is to legislate on. Part of this knowledge can be gained from information available to men in private as well as public stations. Another part can only be gained, or at least thoroughly gained, through actual experience in the post that requires it. In all such cases, therefore, the period of service ought to bear some proportion to the amount of practical knowledge the service requires. In most of the States, as we have seen, the period of legislative service for the more numerous branch is one year. The question can then be put in this simple form: is the proportion of two years to the knowledge needed for federal legislation any greater than that of one year to the knowledge needed for State legislation? The mere statement of the question in this form suggests the answer it deserves.

In a single State, the knowledge needed concerns the existing laws, which are uniform throughout the State and with which all citizens are more or less familiar. It also concerns the general affairs of the State, which lie within a small compass, are not very varied, and take up much of the attention and conversation of every class of people. The great stage of the United States presents a very different scene. The laws are far from uniform; they differ in every State. The public affairs of the Union are scattered across a very large region and are made extremely varied by the local affairs bound up with them. They can hardly be learned correctly anywhere except in the central councils, where the representatives of every part of the empire will bring that knowledge. Yet the members from each State ought to have some knowledge of the affairs, and even the laws, of all the States. How can foreign trade be properly regulated by uniform laws without some acquaintance with the commerce, the ports, the usages and the regulations of the different States? How can trade between the different States be properly regulated without some knowledge of their relative situations in these and other respects? How can taxes be wisely imposed and effectively collected unless they are adapted to the different laws and local circumstances that bear on them in the different States? How can uniform regulations for the militia be properly provided without a similar knowledge of the many internal circumstances that set the States apart from each other? These are the principal objects of federal legislation, and they strongly suggest how much information the representatives must acquire. The other internal objects will call for a proportional amount of information about them.

It is true that all these difficulties will gradually be much reduced. The hardest task will be launching the government properly and forming the original federal code. Improvements on the first drafts will become both easier and fewer each year. Past transactions of the government will be a ready and accurate source of information for new members. The affairs of the Union will become more and more objects of curiosity and conversation among citizens at large. And the growing contact among citizens of different States will do much to spread knowledge of one another's affairs, which will in turn help bring their manners and laws into general likeness. But even after all these reductions, the business of federal legislation must continue to exceed the legislative business of a single State, in both novelty and difficulty, by enough to justify the longer period of service given to those who are to conduct it.

One branch of knowledge belongs among the acquirements of a federal representative and has not yet been mentioned: foreign affairs. In regulating our own commerce he ought to know not only the treaties between the United States and other nations but also the commercial policy and laws of those nations. He ought not to be altogether ignorant of the law of nations, since, so far as it is a proper object of municipal legislation, the federal government holds authority over it. And although the House of Representatives is not directly to take part in foreign negotiations and arrangements, the several branches of public affairs are necessarily connected. Those particular branches will therefore often deserve attention in the ordinary course of legislation, and will sometimes require specific legislative sanction and co-operation. Some of this knowledge may no doubt be gained in a man's study, but some can only come from public sources of information; and all of it will be gained to best effect by practical attention to the subject during actual service in the legislature.

There are other considerations, perhaps of less importance, but still worth noticing. Many of the representatives will have to travel a long way, and will have to make arrangements because of it. For suitable men this might be a much more serious objection to the service if it were limited to a single year than if it ran for two. Nothing can be argued on this point from the case of the delegates to the existing Congress. They are indeed elected annually, but the legislative assemblies treat their re-election almost as a matter of course. The people's election of the representatives would not follow the same principle.

A few of the members, as happens in all such assemblies, will have superior talents. Through frequent re-election they will become members of long standing and thorough masters of the public business, and perhaps not unwilling to use these advantages. The larger the proportion of new members, and the less information the bulk of the members have, the more easily they will fall into the snares laid for them. This remark applies just as much to the relation that will exist between the House of Representatives and the Senate.

Our frequent elections have advantages, even in single States, but mixed in with them is a drawback. Where the States are large and hold only one legislative session a year, spurious elections cannot be investigated and annulled in time for the decision to have its proper effect. If a man can get a return, no matter by what unlawful means, the irregular member takes his seat as a matter of course and is sure to hold it long enough to serve his purposes. Hence a very harmful encouragement is given to using unlawful means to get irregular returns. If elections for the federal legislature were annual, this practice might become a very serious abuse, particularly in the more distant States. Each house is, as it necessarily must be, the judge of the elections, qualifications and returns of its members. Experience may suggest improvements for simplifying and speeding up the process in disputed cases. Even so, so large a part of a year would unavoidably pass before an illegitimate member could be removed from his seat that the prospect of it would do little to check unfair and illicit means of getting a seat.

Taken together, all these considerations warrant us in affirming that biennial elections will be as useful to the affairs of the public as we have seen that they will be safe for the liberty of the people.
